body:
A major multi-religious cave complex

The Ellora Caves, locally known as Verul Leni, are in Maharashtra, near the historic city of Aurangabad. The excavations were made in the basalt rock of the Deccan plateau.

Ellora is distinctive because its principal excavated monuments belong to Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism. The major caves were created over several centuries, broadly from the 6th to the 12th century CE.

The 34 principal caves and their religious groups

The Archaeological Survey of India identifies 34 principal caves commonly visited and studied at Ellora. Their numbering provides an important factual distinction:

  • Caves 1–12: Buddhist caves.
  • Caves 13–29: Hindu or Brahmanical caves.
  • Caves 30–34: Jain caves.

The 34 caves are the commonly identified principal monuments. Additional excavations exist in the wider hill range, so 34 should not be interpreted as the number of every excavation ever made in the area.

Buddhist monuments

The Buddhist group includes monasteries, halls and shrines with Buddha images. Cave 10, known as the Vishvakarma Cave or Carpenter's Cave, is an important Buddhist chaitya hall. Cave 12 is a notable 3-storeyed Buddhist excavation.

Hindu monuments

The Hindu caves contain sculptures principally associated with Shiva and Vishnu. Several are particularly important for large Shaiva representations. Cave 16, the Kailasa Temple, is the most celebrated monument in this group.

Jain monuments

The later Jain group contains shrines and sculptures associated with Jain religious traditions. These caves form part of the same large rock-cut complex but are distinct from the Buddhist and Hindu excavations.

Kailasa Temple: Cave 16

The Kailasa Temple, also called Kailasanatha or Kailashnatha, is a monumental rock-cut Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva. Its construction is mainly associated with the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I, whose reign is conventionally dated to approximately 757–783 CE.

The temple is a major achievement of monolithic architecture. Instead of building a temple by placing stone blocks one above another, the builders removed substantial portions of natural rock until the remaining rock formed an independent-looking temple complex.

Its architectural elements include a large courtyard, a Nandi shrine, gateways, subsidiary shrines and a prominent temple tower or vimana. These parts were not separately constructed with ordinary masonry and then placed into a cave. They emerged through the excavation of the existing rock mass.

Why Kailasa differs from an ordinary cave hall

A typical cave hall is an interior hollow excavated into a hill or cliff. Kailasa is different because its builders also removed rock around the temple, exposing the outside of the carved structure. The result resembles a large structural temple, although its essential mass remains part of the original rock.

This explains why Kailasa and Mahabalipuram's rathas are both described as monolithic monuments, even though they differ greatly in size and form.

Patronage and chronology

The attribution of Kailasa to Krishna I is supported by historical evidence discussed by the Archaeological Survey of India. It does not follow that Krishna I personally commissioned or completed every Buddhist, Hindu and Jain cave at Ellora. The complex developed across different periods and under different patterns of patronage.

Ellora was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983.

Prelims focus

  • Ellora: Maharashtra; Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments.
  • 34 principal caves: Buddhist 1–12, Hindu 13–29, Jain 30–34.
  • Cave 10: Vishvakarma, a Buddhist chaitya hall.
  • Cave 12: a 3-storeyed Buddhist excavation.
  • Cave 16: Kailasa Temple, dedicated to Shiva.
  • Trap: Kailasa is associated with Rashtrakuta Krishna I, not the Pallava builders of Mahabalipuram's rathas.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, pp. 41–43, and Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 85–86; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, p. 107; Archaeological Survey of India, Ellora Caves, sections on cave groups and royal patronage, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ellora Caves, accessed 23 November 2026.]

Location and historical background

Badami, historically known as Vatapi, is in present-day Bagalkot district, Karnataka. It was an important centre of the Early Western Chalukyas.

The famous Badami cave temples were excavated into red sandstone cliffs. Their principal development belongs to the 6th century CE. The caves demonstrate the use of rock-cut architecture for Hindu and Jain worship, rather than for Buddhist monastic accommodation alone.

The 4 principal cave temples

The main Badami group is conventionally described as 4 cave temples. The caves are identified by their religious imagery and their numbered positions within the complex.

CaveMain associationCharacteristic features
1ShaivismShiva as Nataraja, with 18 arms; Ardhanarishvara and other Shaiva imagery.
2VaishnavismVishnu imagery, including Trivikrama and Varaha.
3Predominantly VaishnavaLargest principal cave; Vishnu-related sculpture and an inscription dated 578 CE.
4JainismMahavira and other Jain Tirthankara images.

Cave 1: Shaiva imagery

Cave 1 is especially associated with the remarkable relief of 18-armed Nataraja, a representation of Shiva. Other Shaiva images include Ardhanarishvara, the composite representation of Shiva and Parvati.

The presence of such imagery identifies the cave's principal Shaiva association. The number of arms in the Nataraja relief is a precise visual fact that can help distinguish the monument.

Caves 2 and 3: Vishnu-related imagery

Cave 2 is recognised for representations of Vishnu, including Trivikrama and Varaha. Trivikrama depicts Vishnu's great strides, while Varaha represents the boar incarnation.

Cave 3 is the largest of the principal caves. It is especially associated with Vaishnava imagery, although its sculpture also includes composite or other Hindu forms. An inscription records a foundation connected with Mangalesha in 578 CE.

Cave 4: the Jain cave

Cave 4 is dedicated to the Jain religious tradition. It contains images of Mahavira and other Tirthankaras. A Tirthankara is a revered spiritual teacher in Jainism who shows the path to liberation.

How Badami differs from Ellora

Both Badami and Ellora are major rock-cut religious complexes, but their principal religious groupings differ. Badami's 4 famous cave temples represent Hindu and Jain traditions, whereas Ellora's 34 principal caves include Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments.

Counting qualification

The description of Badami as a group of 4 caves refers to its 4 famous principal cave temples. Other rock-cut remains have also been identified in the area. The conventional examination association is the numbered group of 4.

Prelims focus

  • Badami or Vatapi: Bagalkot district, Karnataka.
  • Dynasty: Early Western Chalukyas.
  • Main complex: 4 principal rock-cut cave temples.
  • Cave 1: Shaiva; 18-armed Nataraja relief.
  • Caves 2 and 3: predominantly Vaishnava; Cave 3 has a 578 CE inscription.
  • Cave 4: Jain, with Mahavira and other Tirthankaras.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 86–87; Government of Karnataka, Bagalkot District Administration, Badami Caves, cave descriptions and inscriptions, accessed 23 November 2026; Karnataka Tourism, Badami, Badami Cave Temples, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The 18-armed Nataraja relief is a defining image of Badami Cave 1.

title: Badami Cave Temples: Chalukyan Rock-cut Architecture

body:
Mahabalipuram under the Pallavas

Mahabalipuram, also called Mamallapuram, is situated on the coast of Tamil Nadu. Its monuments are closely associated with the Pallava dynasty, particularly the reign of Narasimhavarman I, known as Mamalla, who ruled approximately 630–668 CE.

The name Mamallapuram is connected with Mamalla. During the Pallava period, the site became an important centre of rock-cut temples, sculptured rock surfaces and monolithic architectural forms.

What are the Five Rathas?

The Five Rathas, also known as the Pancha Rathas, are a famous group of monolithic rock-cut monuments. Each was carved from a continuous mass of natural rock rather than assembled from separate building blocks.

The word ratha ordinarily means a chariot, but these monuments are temple-shaped architectural forms, not wheeled vehicles. Their traditional names refer to characters from the Mahabharata. Those names should not be mistaken for evidence that the epic characters built the monuments.

Names and principal architectural features

RathaDistinctive form
Dharmaraja RathaMulti-storeyed, pyramidal temple form.
Bhima RathaElongated rectangular form with a wagon-vaulted roof.
Arjuna RathaCompact, multi-tiered shrine form.
Nakula-Sahadeva RathaApsidal or rounded-ended plan.
Draupadi RathaSmall shrine resembling a simple hut.

The different forms show that Pallava artisans explored several temple designs through monolithic carving. A learner can identify the rathas not merely by their names but also by their contrasting outlines.

How a monolithic ratha was created

The builders worked with an existing mass of rock and removed unwanted portions to reveal the architectural form. In contrast to a structural temple, where separate stone blocks are prepared and joined, a monolithic ratha preserves the continuity of the original rock.

Because much of the architectural form was exposed through excavation, the work could proceed downward from the upper portions of the boulder. The finished monument therefore resembles a constructed temple even though its essential body was never assembled from separate pieces.

Rathas, cave mandapas and the Shore Temple

Mahabalipuram contains more than one kind of architecture. Its cave mandapas are halls excavated into natural rock. The rathas are monolithic temple forms. The famous Shore Temple, associated with the later Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman II or Rajasimha, is principally a structural temple complex.

These distinctions matter because a reference to the Pallava monuments at Mahabalipuram does not automatically mean that every monument there was excavated in the same way.

The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984.

Prelims focus

  • Mahabalipuram or Mamallapuram: Tamil Nadu; Pallava dynasty.
  • Narasimhavarman I: known as Mamalla.
  • Pancha Rathas: Dharmaraja, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula-Sahadeva and Draupadi.
  • Bhima Ratha: elongated, wagon-vaulted form.
  • Nakula-Sahadeva Ratha: apsidal form.
  • Trap: The rathas are monolithic temple forms, not actual chariots or monuments constructed by the Pandavas.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, p. 124; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 83–85; Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Monuments Mahabalipuram, sections on the Five Rathas and Pallava rulers, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, accessed 23 November 2026.]

body:
Location and historical setting

The Udayagiri–Khandagiri Caves are situated on 2 neighbouring hills near Bhubaneswar in Odisha. They are important early examples of Jain rock-cut architecture.

The principal early excavations are associated with approximately the 2nd–1st century BCE and with the historical setting of King Kharavela of Kalinga. The caves were created primarily as places of residence, meditation and religious activity for Jain monks.

Unlike the elaborate Buddhist chaitya halls of Ajanta, many caves here consist of relatively small cells or chambers. Some have pillared verandas, decorated entrances and relief carvings.

Udayagiri and Khandagiri: 2 neighbouring hills

The names Udayagiri and Khandagiri refer to separate hills forming one important group of monuments. The site should be studied as a Jain monastic complex rather than as a single cave or an exclusively Buddhist establishment.

Although some excavations were enlarged or modified in subsequent centuries, the early Jain association is central to their historical identity.

Rani Gumpha: an important cave at Udayagiri

Rani Gumpha, meaning Queen's Cave, is among the best-known excavations at Udayagiri. It is a 2-storeyed rock-cut structure with cells, verandas and prominent relief decoration.

The carved scenes include representations associated with courtly and narrative subjects. The structure shows that a cave used by an ascetic community could also possess substantial architectural and sculptural decoration.

What the name does not prove

The conventional name Rani Gumpha should not be taken as proof that the structure was a queen's residence. Its broader archaeological context is that of Jain religious and monastic activity.

Hathigumpha inscription and Kharavela

The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri is an important historical inscription associated with King Kharavela. It provides evidence for the ruler and his activities.

Its significance goes beyond the decoration of a cave. Inscriptions connect monuments with historical persons, political activity and religious patronage. Thus, the association between Kharavela and Udayagiri–Khandagiri is supported by more than a traditional story about the caves.

Distinguishing this complex from similarly named sites

Udayagiri is a name used for more than one Indian heritage location. In the present context, the reference is specifically to Udayagiri and Khandagiri near Bhubaneswar, Odisha, known primarily for Jain caves and the Kharavela inscription.

The correct combination of location, faith and inscription is more reliable than remembering the name Udayagiri alone.

Prelims focus

  • Udayagiri–Khandagiri: near Bhubaneswar, Odisha.
  • Principal religious association: Jainism.
  • Historical ruler: Kharavela of Kalinga.
  • Hathigumpha inscription: associated with Kharavela at Udayagiri.
  • Rani Gumpha: notable 2-storeyed rock-cut cave at Udayagiri.
  • Trap: These Odisha caves should not be identified as the Buddhist caves of Ajanta or the Ajivika caves of Barabar.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, pp. 44–45; Odisha Tourism, Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves, sections Discover the Heritage and Highlights, accessed 23 November 2026.]
